question: Given an Employee table with columns id, name, salary, write a SQL query to return the second highest salary. If there is no second highest salary, return NULL.
thoughtProcess: First I clarify with the interviewer whether they want the second highest distinct salary and how ties at the top should be treated. Almost always they mean distinct values, so two people both at 100k count as one highest. The cleanest mental model is: take the maximum salary among all salaries strictly less than the overall maximum. This returns NULL automatically when no such value exists, because an aggregate over an empty set yields NULL. I will also mention the DISTINCT + ORDER BY + LIMIT/OFFSET alternative, noting it returns zero rows rather than NULL unless wrapped in a scalar subquery.
lineByLine: Line 1 selects the maximum salary from the filtered set and aliases it. The subquery (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee) computes the overall highest salary. The WHERE clause keeps only rows whose salary is strictly less than that maximum, removing everyone tied for first. Taking MAX over the remainder gives the second highest distinct value. If nothing qualifies (only one distinct salary), MAX over an empty set returns NULL.
timeComplexity: O(n) where n is the number of rows. The engine scans once for the inner MAX and once for the outer aggregation; two linear passes without an index.
spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space. Each aggregate tracks a single running maximum with no per-row state.

alternativeApproaches.title: DISTINCT + ORDER BY + LIMIT/OFFSET
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Sort distinct salaries descending and skip the first. Wrap it in an outer SELECT so a missing offset row coerces to NULL instead of returning zero rows.

alternativeApproaches.title: DENSE_RANK window function
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Rank distinct salaries with DENSE_RANK so ties share a rank, then filter for rank 2. This generalizes cleanly to the Nth highest by changing one constant.

followUps.question: How would you generalize this to the Nth highest salary?
followUps.answer: Use DENSE_RANK so ties collapse to a single rank, then filter for the desired rank: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee) t WHERE rnk = N. DENSE_RANK is preferred over ROW_NUMBER because the question is about distinct salary values, not distinct employees. The nested-subquery trick does not generalize because you would need N levels of nesting, whereas the window approach changes only one constant.

followUps.question: Why does the aggregate approach return NULL while LIMIT/OFFSET returns no rows?
followUps.answer: The outer query is an aggregate (MAX) with no GROUP BY, so it always produces exactly one row even over an empty input, and an aggregate over zero rows yields NULL. By contrast, LIMIT/OFFSET on a plain row-returning query produces zero rows when the offset is out of range, which is why you wrap it in a scalar subquery to coerce the empty result into a single NULL.

question: Given an Employee table with columns id, name, salary, write a query that returns the Nth highest distinct salary as a parameterized result. Demonstrate it for N = 3.
thoughtProcess: The interviewer wants a solution that scales to any N, not a hand-written chain of subqueries. The window-function family is the right tool. The key decision is which ranking function: DENSE_RANK collapses ties so the Nth highest means the Nth distinct salary value, which is what the word distinct in the prompt asks for. ROW_NUMBER would treat two people earning the same salary as different ranks, which is wrong here. I rank all rows, then keep the rank equal to N, and use MAX (or DISTINCT) to fold any ties at that rank into a single value. I should note that returning NULL when N exceeds the number of distinct salaries falls out naturally from the aggregate wrapper.
lineByLine: The inner query assigns every row a DENSE_RANK ordered by salary descending; ties receive the same rank and ranks have no gaps. The WHERE clause keeps only rows whose rank equals N (here 3). MAX over those rows returns the single salary value at that rank, and yields NULL if no row reaches rank N. Changing the constant 3 to any N parameterizes the query.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) dominated by the sort required to compute DENSE_RANK over all rows.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer the window function materializes before ranking.

alternativeApproaches.title: LIMIT/OFFSET over distinct salaries
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Select distinct salaries ordered descending and skip N-1 rows. Simple and index-friendly, but it returns zero rows rather than NULL when N is too large unless wrapped in a scalar subquery.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT DISTINCT salary AS NthHighestSalary
FROM Employee
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2;

alternativeApproaches.title: Correlated subquery counting greater salaries
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A salary is the Nth highest if exactly N-1 distinct salaries are strictly greater than it. This is portable to engines without window functions but is O(n^2) in the naive form.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT DISTINCT e.salary AS NthHighestSalary
FROM Employee e
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
       FROM Employee e2
       WHERE e2.salary > e.salary) = 2;

followUps.question: Why DENSE_RANK rather than RANK or ROW_NUMBER here?
followUps.answer: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequence so tied salaries become different ranks, which would make the Nth highest depend on tie-break order rather than on distinct values. RANK leaves gaps after ties (1, 1, 3), so rank N may not exist even when N distinct values do, causing missed answers. DENSE_RANK gives consecutive ranks where each distinct salary maps to exactly one rank, matching the meaning of the Nth highest distinct salary.

followUps.question: How would you wrap this in a reusable function?
followUps.answer: In Postgres or MySQL you can create a function that takes N as an argument and returns the scalar. For example, in MySQL: CREATE FUNCTION getNthHighestSalary(N INT) RETURNS INT BEGIN DECLARE M INT; SET M = N - 1; RETURN (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET M); END. The OFFSET cannot take an expression directly in MySQL, so you precompute N-1 into a variable. The function returns NULL automatically when the offset exceeds available rows.

question: Given Employee(id, name, salary, department_id) and Department(id, name), write a query returning the highest-paid employee in each department. Include all employees tied for the top salary in their department.
thoughtProcess: The phrase include all employees tied tells me to keep ties, so RANK or DENSE_RANK is correct rather than ROW_NUMBER which would arbitrarily keep one. I partition by department so the ranking restarts per group, order by salary descending, and keep rank 1. I then join to Department to expose the department name. I should confirm the desired column names and whether departments with no employees should appear (they will not with an inner join).

solution.code:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM (
  SELECT name, salary, department_id,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM Employee
) e
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE e.rnk = 1;

lineByLine: The inner query ranks employees within each department by salary descending using RANK so ties share rank 1. The outer query joins the ranked set to Department to get the department name. WHERE rnk = 1 keeps every top earner, including all tied employees. Using RANK rather than ROW_NUMBER is what preserves ties.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the partitioned sort, plus the join cost which is typically O(n) with an index on Department.id.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the window-function sort buffer and the join hash table.

alternativeApproaches.title: Correlated subquery with MAX
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Keep each employee whose salary equals the max salary of their department. Naturally returns ties and works on engines without window functions.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(e2.salary)
                  FROM Employee e2
                  WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id);

alternativeApproaches.title: Join to a grouped max derived table
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Precompute the per-department max once, then join employees back to it. This avoids re-evaluating the subquery per row and is often faster than the correlated form.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN (SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal
      FROM Employee GROUP BY department_id) m
  ON m.department_id = e.department_id AND m.max_sal = e.salary
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.department_id;

followUps.question: What changes if you want exactly one employee per department even when there are ties?
followUps.answer: Switch from RANK to ROW_NUMBER and add a deterministic tie-breaker to the ORDER BY, for example ORDER BY salary DESC, id ASC. ROW_NUMBER produces a strict 1..k sequence so exactly one row gets rn = 1 per partition, and the secondary key makes the choice reproducible across runs.

followUps.question: How would you include departments that currently have no employees?
followUps.answer: Replace the inner join with a LEFT JOIN starting from Department: SELECT d.name, e.name, e.salary FROM Department d LEFT JOIN (ranked employees with rnk=1) e ON e.department_id = d.id. Empty departments then appear with NULL employee and salary. With an inner join those departments are dropped because there is no matching employee row.

question: Given Employee(id, name, salary, manager_id) where manager_id references id in the same table, write a query that returns the names of employees who earn strictly more than their direct manager.
thoughtProcess: This is a self-join problem. I join the Employee table to itself: one alias for the employee, one for the manager, matched on employee.manager_id = manager.id. Then I filter where the employee salary exceeds the manager salary. I should confirm whether employees with no manager (NULL manager_id) should be excluded; an inner join naturally drops them, which is correct since they have no manager to compare against.

solution.code:
SELECT e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

lineByLine: The Employee table is aliased twice: e for the worker and m for the manager. The join condition e.manager_id = m.id links each employee to their manager row. The WHERE clause keeps only employees whose salary strictly exceeds their manager's salary. Employees with NULL manager_id never match the join condition and are excluded, which is the intended behavior.
timeComplexity: O(n) with an index on id (lookup per row), or O(n^2) without an index due to the nested-loop self-join.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the hash table if the planner chooses a hash join; O(1) extra for a nested-loop join.

alternativeApproaches.title: Correlated subquery
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For each employee, compare their salary to the salary of the manager fetched by a scalar subquery. Equivalent logic, sometimes clearer to read, but typically less efficient than a join.

followUps.question: How would you also return the manager's name and the salary gap?
followUps.answer: Add the manager alias columns to the SELECT and compute the difference: SELECT e.name AS Employee, m.name AS Manager, e.salary - m.salary AS gap FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary. The self-join already exposes both rows, so you simply project the additional columns.

followUps.question: What if you needed employees earning more than any manager above them in the chain, not just the direct manager?
followUps.answer: That requires traversing the hierarchy with a recursive CTE that walks from each employee up through successive manager_id links, carrying the starting employee's salary, and flagging any ancestor whose salary is lower. A single self-join only compares one level, so it cannot answer questions about indirect managers higher in the org tree.

question: Given a Person table with columns id and email, write a query that returns all email addresses that appear more than once. Return each duplicated email exactly once.
thoughtProcess: Finding duplicates is a GROUP BY plus HAVING problem. I group by the email, count occurrences, and keep only groups whose count exceeds one. HAVING is required rather than WHERE because the filter applies to an aggregate computed after grouping. I should confirm whether emails are case-sensitive; if not, I would group on LOWER(email).

solution.code:
SELECT email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

lineByLine: GROUP BY email collapses all rows sharing the same email into one group. COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only groups with at least two rows, i.e. duplicated emails. The SELECT returns each duplicated email once because grouping already deduplicates.
timeComplexity: O(n) on average using a hash aggregate, or O(n log n) if the engine sorts to group.
spaceComplexity: O(d) where d is the number of distinct emails held in the aggregation hash table.

alternativeApproaches.title: Self-join on equal email and different id
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Two distinct rows with the same email indicate a duplicate. SELECT DISTINCT avoids reporting the same email multiple times. Less efficient than grouping but portable.

alternativeApproaches.title: Window COUNT
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Count occurrences per email without collapsing rows, then filter. Useful when you also need to see the individual duplicate rows.

followUps.question: How would you delete the duplicate rows, keeping the row with the smallest id per email?
followUps.answer: Use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by email ordered by id, then delete rows where the number is greater than 1. In Postgres: DELETE FROM Person WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM Person) t WHERE rn > 1). This keeps the lowest id and removes the rest.

followUps.question: What if emails differ only by letter case but should be treated as the same?
followUps.answer: Normalize before grouping: GROUP BY LOWER(email) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, and SELECT LOWER(email). For a permanent fix you would add a case-insensitive unique constraint, for instance a functional unique index on LOWER(email) in Postgres or a CITEXT column, so duplicates cannot be inserted in the first place.

question: Given a Logins table with columns user_id and login_date (a DATE, at most one row per user per day), write a query that returns the user_ids of every user who logged in on three or more consecutive days.
thoughtProcess: Consecutive-day detection is a classic gaps-and-islands problem. The trick is to subtract a dense row number per user from the date: within a run of consecutive days, login_date minus row_number is constant, so it becomes a group key for the island. I number each user's logins by date, compute the offset date, group by user plus that anchor, and keep groups whose size is at least three. I will mention the LAG-based alternative for explaining the intuition.

solution.code:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM Logins
),
islands AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         login_date - rn * INTERVAL ''1 day'' AS grp
  FROM numbered
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM islands
GROUP BY user_id, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

lineByLine: The numbered CTE assigns each user's logins a sequence by date. In the islands CTE, subtracting rn days from login_date produces a constant anchor for any stretch of consecutive days, because both the date and the counter increase by one each day. Grouping by user_id and that anchor collects each consecutive run into one group; COUNT(*) >= 3 keeps runs of three or more days. DISTINCT user_id returns each qualifying user once even if they have multiple long streaks.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) dominated by the per-user sort needed for ROW_NUMBER.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the window sort and the grouping hash table.

alternativeApproaches.title: Triple self-join on offset dates
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Match a row to rows one and two days later for the same user. Simple to reason about for exactly three days but does not generalize cleanly to longer streaks.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT DISTINCT a.user_id
FROM Logins a
JOIN Logins b ON b.user_id = a.user_id AND b.login_date = a.login_date + INTERVAL ''1 day''
JOIN Logins c ON c.user_id = a.user_id AND c.login_date = a.login_date + INTERVAL ''2 day'';

alternativeApproaches.title: LAG-based run detection
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Flag where a new run starts (gap from previous date > 1 day), take a running sum of those flags as a group id, then count per group. This is the explicit form of the same gaps-and-islands idea.
alternativeApproaches.code:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         CASE WHEN login_date - LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) = INTERVAL ''1 day'' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new
  FROM Logins
),
grouped AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         SUM(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM grouped GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

followUps.question: How would you return the length of each user's longest streak instead of a yes/no?
followUps.answer: Compute the island groups the same way, count rows per (user_id, grp) to get each streak length, then take the maximum per user: SELECT user_id, MAX(streak) FROM (SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS streak FROM islands GROUP BY user_id, grp) s GROUP BY user_id. The outer aggregation collapses multiple streaks per user into the single longest one.

followUps.question: Why subtract a ROW_NUMBER rather than just compare to the previous row?
followUps.answer: Subtracting a dense, gapless ROW_NUMBER from the date turns every consecutive run into rows that share the same constant value, so a single GROUP BY isolates each island in one pass. Comparing to the previous row with LAG only tells you where a run breaks; you still need a running sum to convert those breakpoints into group ids. The ROW_NUMBER trick is a more direct encoding of the same idea and avoids the extra running-sum step.

question: Given a Transactions table with columns id, account_id, txn_date, amount, write a query that returns a running (cumulative) total of amount per account, ordered by date.
thoughtProcess: A running total is the canonical use of SUM as a window function with an ordered frame. I partition by account so each account accumulates independently, order by date so the cumulative sum advances chronologically, and rely on the default frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. I should mention that ties on txn_date with the default RANGE frame include all peer rows at once, so if exact ordering on same-day transactions matters I add a tie-breaker and switch to a ROWS frame.

solution.code:
SELECT account_id, txn_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY account_id
         ORDER BY txn_date
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_total
FROM Transactions
ORDER BY account_id, txn_date;

lineByLine: SUM(amount) OVER (...) computes a cumulative sum. PARTITION BY account_id restarts the total for each account. ORDER BY txn_date defines the accumulation order. The explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW frame sums every row from the partition start up to and including the current row, giving the running total. The final ORDER BY presents the output chronologically per account.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the partitioned sort; the cumulative sum itself is a single linear pass over each ordered partition.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer; the running aggregate keeps O(1) state per partition.

alternativeApproaches.title: Correlated subquery
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For each row, sum all earlier rows of the same account. Portable to engines without window functions but O(n^2) because the subquery rescans per row.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT t.account_id, t.txn_date, t.amount,
       (SELECT SUM(t2.amount) FROM Transactions t2
        WHERE t2.account_id = t.account_id AND t2.txn_date <= t.txn_date) AS running_total
FROM Transactions t
ORDER BY t.account_id, t.txn_date;

followUps.question: What is the difference between a ROWS frame and a RANGE frame for a running total?
followUps.answer: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts physical rows, so each row gets the sum of itself and all prior rows in order. RANGE (the default when you write ORDER BY without a frame) groups by the ORDER BY value, so all rows sharing the current txn_date receive the same cumulative total that includes every tied peer. If two transactions occur on the same date, ROWS distinguishes them by position while RANGE lumps them together. Choose ROWS with a deterministic tie-breaker when same-day ordering matters.

followUps.question: How would you reset the running total at the start of each calendar year?
followUps.answer: Add the year to the partition key so accumulation restarts annually: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM txn_date) ORDER BY txn_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Partitioning by year means the cumulative sum begins again at zero each January for every account.

question: Given a Sales table with columns sale_month (a DATE on the first of each month) and revenue, write a query returning each month's revenue, the previous month's revenue, and the month-over-month percentage growth.
thoughtProcess: Month-over-month growth compares each row to the immediately preceding period. LAG is the natural tool: it fetches the prior row's revenue when ordered by month. Growth is (current - previous) / previous expressed as a percent. I must guard against division by zero or NULL for the first month, where there is no previous value, by using NULLIF on the denominator so the result becomes NULL rather than an error. I should confirm months are contiguous; if some months are missing, LAG would compare to the nearest existing month, not the true previous calendar month, which I would address with a calendar dimension.

solution.code:
SELECT sale_month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY sale_month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(
         100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY sale_month))
         / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY sale_month), 0), 2
       ) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM Sales
ORDER BY sale_month;

lineByLine: LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY sale_month) returns the revenue of the previous month. The growth expression subtracts the previous from the current, divides by the previous, and multiplies by 100 for a percentage. NULLIF(..., 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL so the division does not error. ROUND trims to two decimals. The first month has no previous row, so LAG returns NULL and the growth is NULL.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the ordering the window requires; the LAG lookups are O(1) per row.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer.

alternativeApproaches.title: Self-join on previous month
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Join each month to the row exactly one month earlier. Works without window functions but requires explicit date arithmetic and is harder to read.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT c.sale_month, c.revenue, p.revenue AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (c.revenue - p.revenue) / NULLIF(p.revenue, 0), 2) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM Sales c
LEFT JOIN Sales p ON p.sale_month = c.sale_month - INTERVAL ''1 month''
ORDER BY c.sale_month;

followUps.question: How would you compute year-over-year growth instead?
followUps.answer: Compare each month to the same month a year earlier. With LAG you offset by 12 positions assuming contiguous monthly data: LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY sale_month). More robustly, self-join on p.sale_month = c.sale_month - INTERVAL '1 year', which is correct even if some months are missing because it matches by actual date rather than by row count.

followUps.question: What problem arises if some months have no rows, and how do you fix it?
followUps.answer: LAG compares to the previous existing row, not the previous calendar month, so a gap silently produces a wrong comparison (for example February compared to December if January is missing). The fix is to left-join against a generated calendar of all months, filling missing revenue with zero or NULL, so that LAG always steps exactly one month. A calendar dimension table or a generate_series of month starts provides that dense spine.

question: Given Employee(id, salary, department_id), write a query that returns the median salary for each department. Handle both odd and even group sizes correctly.
thoughtProcess: Median is awkward in SQL because there is no universal MEDIAN aggregate. The portable approach ranks salaries within each department from both ends and averages the middle one or two values. A clean trick is to compute, per department, the row number ascending and the count, then keep rows whose position is within one of the center: position in (floor((cnt+1)/2), ceil((cnt+1)/2)) wait, more simply abs(2*rn - cnt - 1) < 2 selects the one middle row for odd sizes and the two middle rows for even sizes, and averaging them gives the median. If the engine has PERCENTILE_CONT I would prefer it for clarity.

solution.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT department_id, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) AS cnt
  FROM Employee
)
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((cnt + 1) / 2.0), CEIL((cnt + 1) / 2.0))
GROUP BY department_id;

lineByLine: The ranked CTE numbers salaries ascending within each department and also exposes the department's row count. The WHERE clause keeps the middle position(s): for an odd count, FLOOR and CEIL of (cnt+1)/2 are equal, selecting one row; for an even count they differ by one, selecting the two central rows. AVG over those rows yields the median, equal to the single middle value for odd sizes and the mean of the two middle values for even sizes. GROUP BY collapses to one median per department.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the per-department ordering; the rest is linear filtering and aggregation.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the window sort.

alternativeApproaches.title: PERCENTILE_CONT ordered-set aggregate
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Postgres, Oracle, Snowflake, and BigQuery support PERCENTILE_CONT, which interpolates the 50th percentile and handles even sizes by averaging automatically. The clearest option when available.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT department_id,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS median_salary
FROM Employee
GROUP BY department_id;

alternativeApproaches.title: Symmetric ranking from both ends
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Rank ascending and descending; the median rows are those where the two ranks are within one of each other. Avoids needing the count explicitly.
alternativeApproaches.code:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT department_id, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary) AS asc_rn,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS desc_rn
  FROM Employee
)
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM r
WHERE asc_rn BETWEEN desc_rn - 1 AND desc_rn + 1
GROUP BY department_id;

followUps.question: Why can you not just use AVG to approximate the median?
followUps.answer: AVG computes the arithmetic mean, which is the average value, not the middle value. The two diverge whenever the distribution is skewed: a department with salaries 30k, 35k, 40k, 200k has a mean near 76k but a median of 37.5k. Interviewers ask for median precisely because it resists outliers, so substituting AVG gives a numerically different and often misleading answer.

followUps.question: What is the difference between PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCENTILE_DISC?
followUps.answer: PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between adjacent values, so the median of an even-sized set is the average of the two middle values, which can be a number not present in the data. PERCENTILE_DISC returns an actual existing value, picking the first value whose cumulative distribution reaches the requested percentile. For median, PERCENTILE_CONT matches the textbook definition that averages the two central values, while PERCENTILE_DISC would return one of them.

question: Given a table Numbers with a single integer column n that has gaps in the sequence, write a query that returns the start and end of each consecutive range of present values. For example values 1,2,3,5,6,9 produce ranges 1-3, 5-6, 9-9.
thoughtProcess: This is the gaps-and-islands pattern applied to integers. Within a consecutive run, the value minus its dense row number is constant, so that difference identifies each island. I order all values, assign a ROW_NUMBER, subtract it from n to form a group key, then take MIN and MAX of n per group to get the range bounds. I will mention the LAG/running-sum alternative which is equivalent but more verbose.

solution.code:
WITH g AS (
  SELECT n,
         n - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY n) AS grp
  FROM Numbers
)
SELECT MIN(n) AS range_start, MAX(n) AS range_end
FROM g
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY range_start;

lineByLine: The CTE g computes n minus its position in the ordered sequence. For any run of consecutive integers, both n and the row number increase by one per step, so their difference stays constant across the whole run and changes only at a gap. Grouping by grp therefore collects each consecutive range into one group. MIN(n) and MAX(n) give the first and last value of each range, and the final ORDER BY presents them in ascending order.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the single ordered window pass; grouping is linear after that.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer and group hash table.

alternativeApproaches.title: LAG/LEAD boundary detection
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A range starts where the previous value is not n-1 and ends where the next value is not n+1. Pairing starts with the next end reconstructs the ranges. More explicit but wordier.
alternativeApproaches.code:
WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT n,
         CASE WHEN LAG(n) OVER (ORDER BY n) = n - 1 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_start,
         SUM(CASE WHEN LAG(n) OVER (ORDER BY n) = n - 1 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END) OVER (ORDER BY n) AS grp
  FROM Numbers
)
SELECT MIN(n) AS range_start, MAX(n) AS range_end
FROM bounds GROUP BY grp ORDER BY range_start;

followUps.question: How would you instead find the missing gaps (the values absent between ranges)?
followUps.answer: Use LEAD to look at the next present value; wherever next - current > 1 there is a gap, and the missing range is current+1 through next-1: SELECT n + 1 AS gap_start, LEAD(n) OVER (ORDER BY n) - 1 AS gap_end FROM Numbers WHERE LEAD(n) OVER (ORDER BY n) - n > 1. Each qualifying row describes one stretch of missing integers between two islands.

followUps.question: Does the ROW_NUMBER trick work for dates as well as integers?
followUps.answer: Yes, with one adjustment: subtract ROW_NUMBER days from the date rather than a raw integer, for example login_date - rn * INTERVAL '1 day'. Because dates advance by a constant unit just like integers, the difference remains constant across a consecutive run. The same gaps-and-islands grouping then isolates each unbroken date range.

question: Given a Scores table with columns category and score, write a query that returns the top 3 scores within each category, ordered highest first.
thoughtProcess: Top-N per group is the prototypical use of a ranking window function. I partition by category, order by score descending, assign a number, and keep the first three. The choice between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK depends on tie handling, so I clarify that with the interviewer. ROW_NUMBER returns exactly three rows even with ties; DENSE_RANK returns all rows in the top three distinct scores, which may be more than three rows. I default to ROW_NUMBER for an exact top 3 and add a tie-breaker for determinism.

solution.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, score,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY score DESC) AS rn
  FROM Scores
)
SELECT category, score
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, score DESC;

lineByLine: The ranked CTE numbers rows within each category by score descending. PARTITION BY category restarts numbering per group. ROW_NUMBER gives a strict 1..k sequence. WHERE rn <= 3 keeps the three highest per category. The final ORDER BY presents results grouped by category with the highest scores first.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the per-partition sort.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the window sort buffer.

alternativeApproaches.title: Correlated count subquery
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Keep a row if fewer than three scores in its category are strictly greater. Portable to engines without window functions but O(n^2).
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT s.category, s.score
FROM Scores s
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Scores s2
       WHERE s2.category = s.category AND s2.score > s.score) < 3
ORDER BY s.category, s.score DESC;

alternativeApproaches.title: Lateral / cross apply
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For each distinct category, fetch its top 3 with a LATERAL subquery using ORDER BY and LIMIT. Efficient when an index supports the per-category ordering.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT c.category, t.score
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM Scores) c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT score FROM Scores s
  WHERE s.category = c.category
  ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 3
) t;

followUps.question: How does the result change if you use DENSE_RANK instead of ROW_NUMBER?
followUps.answer: DENSE_RANK keeps all rows belonging to the top three distinct score values, so ties are preserved and a category can return more than three rows (for example five rows if the third-highest score is shared by three people). ROW_NUMBER returns exactly three rows, arbitrarily breaking ties. Pick DENSE_RANK when the requirement is the top three score levels including ties, and ROW_NUMBER when it is strictly three rows.

followUps.question: How would you make ROW_NUMBER deterministic when scores tie?
followUps.answer: Add a stable secondary key to the ORDER BY, such as a unique id: ORDER BY score DESC, id ASC. Without it, two rows with equal scores can swap positions between executions, so which one lands in the top 3 becomes non-deterministic. A deterministic tie-breaker guarantees the same output for the same input, which matters for reproducible reports and tests.

question: Given a Sales table with columns year, quarter (1-4), and amount, write a query that pivots the data so each row is one year with four columns Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 holding that quarter's total amount.
thoughtProcess: Pivoting rows to columns is conditional aggregation: group by the row dimension (year) and use a CASE inside an aggregate to route each quarter's value into its own column. SUM with a CASE that returns the amount only for the matching quarter and zero or NULL otherwise produces one column per quarter. I prefer SUM over MAX when multiple rows per quarter should accumulate. Some engines have a PIVOT operator, which I will mention as a cleaner alternative where available.

solution.code:
SELECT year,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 1 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS q1,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 2 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS q2,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 3 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS q3,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 4 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS q4
FROM Sales
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year;

lineByLine: GROUP BY year creates one output row per year. Each SUM(CASE ...) adds amount only for the targeted quarter and contributes zero otherwise, so the total for that quarter lands in its dedicated column. Repeating the pattern for quarters 1 through 4 produces the four pivoted columns. ORDER BY year sorts the report.
timeComplexity: O(n) for a single grouped pass over the rows.
spaceComplexity: O(y) where y is the number of distinct years held in the aggregation.

alternativeApproaches.title: Native PIVOT operator
alternativeApproaches.explanation: SQL Server, Oracle, and Snowflake offer a PIVOT clause that expresses this declaratively without writing four CASE expressions.

followUps.question: How would you unpivot these four columns back into rows?
followUps.answer: Use a UNION ALL that emits one row per quarter, or a native UNPIVOT operator. With UNION ALL: SELECT year, 1 AS quarter, q1 AS amount FROM pivoted UNION ALL SELECT year, 2, q2 FROM pivoted UNION ALL ... and so on for q3 and q4. Each branch turns a column into rows, and concatenating them reconstructs the long format.

followUps.question: What if the set of quarters or categories is not known in advance?
followUps.answer: Static CASE pivoting requires knowing the columns at query-write time. For a dynamic set you must build the SQL string at runtime: query the distinct values, generate the CASE or PIVOT column list programmatically, then execute the constructed statement with dynamic SQL (EXECUTE in Postgres, sp_executesql in SQL Server). Pure SQL cannot return a variable number of columns from a single static query.

question: Given Customers(id, name) and Orders(id, customer_id), write a query returning the names of customers who have never placed an order.
thoughtProcess: This is an anti-join: rows in Customers with no matching row in Orders. There are three common ways: LEFT JOIN with an IS NULL filter, NOT EXISTS, and NOT IN. I lead with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL because it is widely understood and performs well. I will warn that NOT IN is dangerous when the subquery can return NULLs, since a single NULL makes the whole NOT IN evaluate to unknown and return no rows.

solution.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

lineByLine: The LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and attaches matching orders, filling order columns with NULL when a customer has none. WHERE o.id IS NULL keeps only the customers for whom no order matched, since a real order would have a non-null id. The result is exactly the customers with zero orders.
timeComplexity: O(n + m) with indexes on the join keys using a hash or merge join; n customers and m orders.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the hash table on the smaller side of the join.

alternativeApproaches.title: NOT EXISTS
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Often the clearest semantically and NULL-safe. The optimizer typically executes it as an anti-join, matching the LEFT JOIN plan.

alternativeApproaches.title: NOT IN (use with caution)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Readable but breaks if the subquery returns any NULL, because NOT IN with a NULL yields unknown for every row. Add a NOT NULL filter to make it safe.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT name FROM Customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM Orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL);

followUps.question: Why can NOT IN silently return zero rows here?
followUps.answer: If the subquery returns even one NULL customer_id, then for any candidate id the expression id NOT IN (..., NULL, ...) evaluates to unknown rather than true, because SQL cannot confirm the id differs from an unknown value. Unknown is not true, so no rows pass the filter and the query returns nothing. NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL do not have this trap, which is why they are preferred for anti-joins.

followUps.question: How would you instead count orders per customer including those with zero?
followUps.answer: Use a LEFT JOIN and COUNT the order key, which counts non-null matches: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name. COUNT(o.id) returns 0 for customers with no orders because COUNT ignores NULLs, whereas COUNT(*) would incorrectly return 1 for them.

question: Given a Results table with columns player and points, write a query that assigns a competition rank to each player ordered by points descending, where players with equal points share the same rank and the next rank skips accordingly (standard competition ranking, e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4).
thoughtProcess: The phrase share the same rank and skip accordingly is the precise definition of RANK, as opposed to DENSE_RANK which does not skip, or ROW_NUMBER which never ties. So the core answer is RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC). I will contrast all three ranking functions because interviewers almost always probe the distinction next.

solution.code:
SELECT player, points,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS competition_rank
FROM Results
ORDER BY competition_rank, player;

lineByLine: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) assigns 1 to the highest points; tied players receive the same rank, and the following rank jumps by the number of tied rows, producing the 1, 2, 2, 4 pattern. The final ORDER BY presents players in rank order with a stable secondary sort by name.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the single ordered window pass.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer.

alternativeApproaches.title: Correlated count subquery
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A player's competition rank equals one plus the number of players with strictly higher points. Reproduces RANK semantics without window functions.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT r.player, r.points,
       1 + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Results r2 WHERE r2.points > r.points) AS competition_rank
FROM Results r
ORDER BY competition_rank, r.player;

followUps.question: Contrast RANK, DENSE_RANK, and ROW_NUMBER on the input 90, 90, 80.
followUps.answer: RANK gives 1, 1, 3: ties share rank 1 and the next rank skips to 3. DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2: ties share rank 1 but the next rank does not skip. ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3: every row gets a unique number with ties broken arbitrarily. Use RANK for standard competition ranking, DENSE_RANK when you want consecutive rank labels, and ROW_NUMBER when you need a strict unique sequence.

followUps.question: How would you compute a percentile rank instead?
followUps.answer: Use PERCENT_RANK or CUME_DIST window functions. PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) returns (rank - 1) / (total rows - 1), giving a value from 0 to 1. CUME_DIST returns the cumulative fraction of rows at or beyond the current value. These express relative standing as a proportion rather than an integer position, which is useful for comparing across differently sized groups.

question: Given an Events table with columns user_id and event_time (timestamp), define a session as a maximal run of a user's events where each consecutive pair is no more than 30 minutes apart. Write a query that assigns a session_id to every event.
thoughtProcess: Sessionization by an inactivity gap is gaps-and-islands on timestamps. For each user ordered by time, I use LAG to get the previous event time and flag a new session whenever the gap exceeds 30 minutes (or there is no previous event). A running SUM of those flags within the user partition produces a monotonically increasing session number. I combine it with user_id to make a globally unique session id. The 30-minute threshold is the only business parameter.

solution.code:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_time,
         CASE WHEN event_time - LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time)
                   > INTERVAL ''30 minutes''
              OR LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) IS NULL
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
  FROM Events
)
SELECT user_id, event_time,
       user_id || ''-'' ||
       SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time
                                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS session_id
FROM flagged
ORDER BY user_id, event_time;

lineByLine: The flagged CTE uses LAG to find each event's previous event time per user. The CASE sets is_new_session to 1 when the gap exceeds 30 minutes or there is no previous event (the user's first event), otherwise 0. In the outer query, a running SUM of is_new_session within the user partition increments at each new session boundary, producing a per-user session sequence 1, 2, 3, .... Concatenating user_id with that number yields a globally unique session_id. ORDER BY presents events chronologically per user.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the per-user ordered window passes.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffers; running state per partition is O(1).

alternativeApproaches.title: Single window with conditional sum inline
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Combine the LAG comparison and the running sum without a CTE on engines that allow nesting window functions through a subquery. Functionally identical; the CTE form is usually clearer.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT user_id, event_time,
       SUM(CASE WHEN gap > INTERVAL ''30 minutes'' OR gap IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
         OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS session_no
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, event_time,
         event_time - LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS gap
  FROM Events
) t;

followUps.question: How would you aggregate to one row per session with start, end, and event count?
followUps.answer: Wrap the sessionized result and group by user_id and session_id: SELECT user_id, session_id, MIN(event_time) AS session_start, MAX(event_time) AS session_end, COUNT(*) AS events, MAX(event_time) - MIN(event_time) AS duration FROM sessionized GROUP BY user_id, session_id. MIN and MAX give the session boundaries, and their difference gives the active duration.

followUps.question: Why is the gap measured between consecutive events rather than from the session start?
followUps.answer: The standard inactivity definition closes a session only after a period of no activity, so each new event within 30 minutes of the previous one extends the session indefinitely. Measuring from the session start instead would cap every session at a fixed length regardless of ongoing activity, which does not match how analytics tools like GA define sessions. The LAG-based consecutive gap correctly implements the rolling-timeout semantics.

question: Given an Events table with columns user_id, event_type, and event_time, write a query that returns, for each user, the event_type of their first event and the event_type of their last event by time.
thoughtProcess: First and last event per user is a job for FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE, or equivalently for two ROW_NUMBER passes. The subtle pitfall with LAST_VALUE is the default frame: it only sees up to the current row, so it returns the current row's value, not the partition's last. I must set the frame to the full partition (ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) for LAST_VALUE to be correct. Then I deduplicate to one row per user with DISTINCT or by grouping.

solution.code:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(event_type) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS first_event,
       LAST_VALUE(event_type) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_event
FROM Events;

lineByLine: FIRST_VALUE returns the event_type of the earliest event in each user's partition. LAST_VALUE returns the event_type of the latest event, but only because the explicit frame ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING widens the window to the entire partition; without it LAST_VALUE would default to the current row. Both window functions produce the same value for every row in a partition, so DISTINCT collapses each user to a single output row.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the per-user sort.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer; DISTINCT adds a hash for deduplication.

alternativeApproaches.title: Two ROW_NUMBER passes
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Number events ascending and descending per user; the first event is rn_asc = 1 and the last is rn_desc = 1. Join or conditionally aggregate to one row. Avoids the LAST_VALUE frame pitfall.
alternativeApproaches.code:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_type,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS rn_asc,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time DESC) AS rn_desc
  FROM Events
)
SELECT user_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn_asc = 1 THEN event_type END) AS first_event,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn_desc = 1 THEN event_type END) AS last_event
FROM r GROUP BY user_id;

followUps.question: Why does LAST_VALUE often return the wrong value if you forget the frame?
followUps.answer: When you specify ORDER BY without an explicit frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That frame ends at the current row, so LAST_VALUE returns the value of the current row rather than the partition's final row. To get the true last value you must extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or sidestep the issue by using FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY event_time DESC.

followUps.question: How would you break ties when two events share the same event_time?
followUps.answer: Add a deterministic secondary key to the ORDER BY, such as an auto-increment id or event sequence: ORDER BY event_time, id. Without it, two events at the identical timestamp could be considered first or last non-deterministically. The tie-breaker ensures the same input always yields the same first and last events.

question: Given a DailyMetrics table with columns metric_date (one row per day) and value, write a query that returns a 7-day moving average of value, where each day's average covers that day and the six days before it.
thoughtProcess: A trailing moving average is AVG as a window function over a row-bounded frame of the current row plus the six preceding rows: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. I use ROWS (physical rows) and assume one row per day so the window spans exactly seven calendar days. If days can be missing, ROWS would average seven existing rows that span more than seven calendar days, so I would switch to a RANGE frame with an interval, or densify the calendar first. I will note that the first six days have fewer than seven rows, so their average covers only the rows available.

solution.code:
SELECT metric_date, value,
       AVG(value) OVER (
         ORDER BY metric_date
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM DailyMetrics
ORDER BY metric_date;

lineByLine: AVG(value) OVER (...) computes an average over a sliding window. ORDER BY metric_date defines the chronological order. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW restricts each calculation to the current day and the six prior rows, a seven-row window. Because there is one row per day, this is a 7-day trailing average. Early dates with fewer than seven preceding rows average only the rows that exist.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the ordering; the sliding window itself is computed incrementally in linear time.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sort buffer; the frame keeps O(window size) running state.

alternativeApproaches.title: Date-range RANGE frame (gap-safe)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use a RANGE frame keyed on an interval so the window covers the last 7 calendar days regardless of missing rows. Correct when some days have no row.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT metric_date, value,
       AVG(value) OVER (
         ORDER BY metric_date
         RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL ''6 days'' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM DailyMetrics
ORDER BY metric_date;

alternativeApproaches.title: Self-join window
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Join each day to the rows within the prior six days and average. Portable to engines without window frames but quadratic in cost.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT a.metric_date, AVG(b.value) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM DailyMetrics a
JOIN DailyMetrics b
  ON b.metric_date BETWEEN a.metric_date - INTERVAL ''6 days'' AND a.metric_date
GROUP BY a.metric_date
ORDER BY a.metric_date;

followUps.question: When would ROWS and RANGE produce different 7-day averages?
followUps.answer: They diverge whenever the data has missing days or duplicate dates. ROWS counts physical rows, so with a missing day it averages seven existing rows that actually span more than seven calendar days. RANGE keyed on an interval averages every row within the literal 7-day date window, correctly excluding the missing day and including duplicates on the same date. With exactly one row per consecutive day they give identical results.

followUps.question: How would you require a full 7-day window, returning NULL for the first six days?
followUps.answer: Compute the count of rows in the frame and null out partial windows: CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) = 7 THEN AVG(value) OVER (same frame) END. The CASE suppresses the average until seven rows are available, so early dates with incomplete windows return NULL instead of a partial average.

question: Given an Orders table with columns category and amount, write a query that returns each category's total amount and that total as a percentage of the grand total across all categories.
thoughtProcess: Percent of total compares a group's aggregate to the overall aggregate. The cleanest approach computes the per-category sum, then divides by an unpartitioned window SUM that spans every row, all in one pass. The window SUM OVER () with no partition gives the grand total alongside each group. I guard the division with NULLIF in case the grand total is zero, and multiply by 100 for a percentage.

solution.code:
SELECT category,
       SUM(amount) AS category_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(amount) / NULLIF(SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (), 0), 2) AS pct_of_total
FROM Orders
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY pct_of_total DESC;

lineByLine: GROUP BY category produces one row per category with SUM(amount) as its total. The expression SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () is a window aggregate applied on top of the grouped result: the inner SUM(amount) is the per-category total and the outer SUM() OVER () adds those category totals into the grand total, repeated on every row. Dividing the category total by the grand total and multiplying by 100 gives the percentage; NULLIF avoids division by zero. ORDER BY ranks categories by share.
timeComplexity: O(n) for the grouped aggregation, plus a linear pass for the window over the grouped rows.
spaceComplexity: O(c) where c is the number of categories.

alternativeApproaches.title: Cross join to a grand-total subquery
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Compute the grand total once in a subquery and cross join it to the per-category totals. Works on engines without window functions.
alternativeApproaches.code:
SELECT g.category, g.category_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * g.category_total / NULLIF(t.grand_total, 0), 2) AS pct_of_total
FROM (SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS category_total FROM Orders GROUP BY category) g
CROSS JOIN (SELECT SUM(amount) AS grand_total FROM Orders) t
ORDER BY pct_of_total DESC;

followUps.question: How would you compute percent of total within each region separately?
followUps.answer: Partition the window total by region so each category's share is relative to its region rather than the whole dataset: 100.0 * SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (PARTITION BY region), grouping by region and category. The PARTITION BY confines the grand total to each region, so percentages sum to 100 within every region.

followUps.question: Why use SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () rather than a separate subquery?
followUps.answer: Because the query already groups by category, the window function operates on the grouped rows: the inner SUM is the per-group aggregate and the outer windowed SUM totals those groups, giving the grand total without a second scan of the base table. A separate subquery would rescan or rejoin the data, so the window approach is usually fewer passes and more concise, while remaining correct.

question: Given an Employee table with columns id, name, and manager_id (a self-reference; the CEO has manager_id NULL), write a query that returns every employee along with their depth level in the org chart, where the CEO is level 1.
thoughtProcess: Traversing an arbitrary-depth hierarchy requires a recursive CTE because the number of levels is not known in advance and a fixed number of self-joins cannot handle it. The anchor member selects the root (manager_id IS NULL) at level 1. The recursive member joins the CTE to Employee on manager_id = parent id, incrementing the level each step. The recursion terminates naturally when no rows have a parent in the previous level. I should mention guarding against cycles in real data with a path or a depth cap.

solution.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
  FROM Employee
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1
  FROM Employee e
  JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT id, name, level
FROM org
ORDER BY level, id;

lineByLine: The anchor member selects the CEO, the row whose manager_id is NULL, and labels it level 1. UNION ALL combines the anchor with the recursive member. The recursive member joins Employee to the running org result, matching each employee to their manager already in org, and sets that employee's level to the manager's level plus one. The engine repeats the recursive step until it produces no new rows, having visited every reachable employee. The outer query projects id, name, and level.
timeComplexity: O(n) per level visited; overall O(n * d) in the worst case where d is the tree depth, though typically close to O(n) since each employee is produced once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) to hold the accumulating recursive result.

alternativeApproaches.title: Recursive CTE carrying a path
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Accumulate the chain of ids or names so you also get the full reporting path, and use it to detect cycles by checking whether an id already appears in the path.
alternativeApproaches.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level, CAST(name AS VARCHAR(1000)) AS path
  FROM Employee WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1, o.path || '' > '' || e.name
  FROM Employee e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT id, name, level, path FROM org ORDER BY level, id;

followUps.question: How would you return only the subtree under a specific manager?
followUps.answer: Change the anchor member to start at that manager instead of the root: WHERE id = :manager_id, keeping the same recursive member. The recursion then walks downward only from that node, producing the manager and all direct and indirect reports beneath them, with levels relative to that starting point.

followUps.question: What happens if the data contains a cycle, and how do you protect against it?
followUps.answer: A cycle (A reports to B and B reports to A) makes a plain recursive CTE loop indefinitely or until the engine's recursion limit aborts it. Protect against it by carrying an array or string path of visited ids and adding a recursive condition like WHERE NOT e.id = ANY(path), or by using the engine's CYCLE clause (Postgres) or MAXRECURSION hint (SQL Server). These stop the recursion when a node would repeat, preventing infinite loops.

question: Given a Friendship table with columns user_a and user_b where each row records that two users are friends, write a query that returns all unique unordered friend pairs, avoiding duplicate pairs like (1,2) and (2,1) and avoiding self-pairs.
thoughtProcess: Finding unordered pairs without duplicates is a self-join with an inequality on the key. If the table stores each friendship once in arbitrary order, I just need to canonicalize so (1,2) and (2,1) are not both returned. The standard trick is to enforce user_a < user_b. If instead the question is about deriving pairs from a membership-style table (users who share something), I self-join on the shared attribute with a.id < b.id to generate each pair once and skip self-pairs. I will present the canonical-ordering self-join, which is the most common framing.

solution.code:
SELECT LEAST(user_a, user_b) AS u1,
       GREATEST(user_a, user_b) AS u2
FROM Friendship
WHERE user_a <> user_b
GROUP BY LEAST(user_a, user_b), GREATEST(user_a, user_b);

lineByLine: LEAST and GREATEST canonicalize each row so the smaller id is always u1 and the larger is u2, collapsing (1,2) and (2,1) into the same pair. WHERE user_a <> user_b removes self-pairs. GROUP BY on the canonical pair deduplicates rows that represent the same friendship recorded twice. The result is each unordered pair exactly once.
timeComplexity: O(n) on average for the hash-based grouping, or O(n log n) if the engine sorts.
spaceComplexity: O(p) where p is the number of distinct pairs in the aggregation.

alternativeApproaches.title: Self-join to find shared-attribute pairs
alternativeApproaches.explanation: When deriving pairs from a table like Enrollment(student, course), self-join on the shared course with student id ordering to produce each classmate pair once.

alternativeApproaches.title: DISTINCT with canonical ordering
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If the friendship table never duplicates a pair, you can skip the GROUP BY and use DISTINCT over the canonicalized columns.

followUps.question: Why does the a.id < b.id condition avoid both duplicates and self-pairs at once?
followUps.answer: The strict inequality a.id < b.id keeps only one ordering of each pair, so (1,2) is produced but (2,1) is excluded, eliminating mirrored duplicates. It also excludes self-pairs automatically, because a row cannot satisfy a.id < a.id. Using <= instead would reintroduce self-pairs, and = would only return self-pairs, so strict less-than is exactly right for unordered distinct pairs.

followUps.question: How would you count the number of mutual friends between every pair of users?
followUps.answer: Self-join the friendship edges so two users are linked through a common friend, then group by the user pair and count distinct common friends. For example, treating friendships as directed edges in both directions, join f1 and f2 on f1.friend = f2.friend with f1.user < f2.user, group by (f1.user, f2.user), and COUNT(DISTINCT f1.friend). Each group's count is the number of mutual friends shared by that pair.
